explanation: Both models fail on the same boundary ambiguity: the label treats 'Bonuses (0)' as a single column value (name with zero-count annotation), but Qwen splits it into 'Bonuses' and '(0)' as two separate columns. T5 correctly keeps 'Bonuses (0)' intact for the first 7 rows but both models split the last row 'Salaries in USD||Average||$52k $54k $56k' — T5 adds an extra split there as well, and neither matches the label exactly due to this final-row inconsistency. The root failure is inability to recognize that '(0)' is part of the bonus category name rather than an independent value column.

Both models identify column boundaries correctly (name, position, height, weight, DOB, status, city, college, years), but Qwen uses ' || ' with spaces while the label expects '||' without spaces, causing exact-match failure for Qwen. T5 merges the player name and position code (e.g. 'Jerrial Dawson G') into the first column instead of separating them, which is a structural segmentation error. They fail differently: Qwen's content is correct but uses wrong delimiter spacing; T5 gets the delimiter right but makes a structural boundary error on the name/position field.

Both models correctly identify the three-column structure (letter grade, first value, second value) across all six rows. The table is simple with clear numeric values and short letter keys, making segmentation straightforward. Qwen uses ' || ' spacing while T5 uses '||', but the evaluator accepts both formats. No notable differences in approach beyond delimiter style.

Both models correctly parse the real-estate listing rows with eight columns (address, lot size, type, price, date, beds, baths, sqft). The consistent structure across rows makes column segmentation unambiguous. Qwen again uses ' || ' padding while T5 uses '||', but both are scored correct. No meaningful difference in approach.

This table has a multi-level header with a colspan row ('&nbsp||Team Stats||Opp Stats' spanning 14 columns filled with empty cells) and many empty trailing cells for future games. Qwen attempts to reproduce the header row but uses incorrect spacing and collapses the empty trailing cells, breaking column count consistency. T5 completely drops the header row's '&nbsp' prefix and merges the header label columns without any separators, producing a structurally invalid first row. Both fail because neither model can handle HTML-style colspan annotations and degenerate empty-cell rows.

The label separates home team, home score, dash, away score, and away team into distinct columns (e.g. 'Schalke||0||-||3||Chelsea'), but both models merge the score with the dash into a single 'score' cell (e.g. '0 - 3'). Qwen additionally uses ' || ' spacing throughout. T5 further merges the row number with the home team name (e.g. '2 Schalke'). Both fail because they cannot distinguish the dash separator in the score from a simple textual dash, collapsing three columns into one.

The label treats 'Player - Position' (e.g. 'Justin Upton - RF') as a single first column, but Qwen splits on the dash creating 'Justin Upton' and '- RF' as two separate columns. T5 keeps the player-position combined correctly but then splits each percentage value from its '%' sign into two separate columns (e.g. '42.9' and '%'), doubling the column count. Both fail but in opposite ways: Qwen over-splits on the name/position hyphen while T5 over-splits on the numeric/symbol boundary within percentage values.

Both models correctly identify the four-column structure (country/chart, peak position, certification, sales) for this album certification table. The data is well-structured with consistent patterns, making segmentation straightforward. Both produce identical content; Qwen uses '||' without spaces here matching the label exactly.

Both models correctly parse the train schedule table with seven columns (stop number, station name with code, arrival, departure, halt duration, zone, distance). The structure is clear and consistent across rows. Qwen uses ' || ' spacing but the evaluator accepts it; T5 uses '||'. No notable differences in approach.

Both models identify the correct four-column structure and produce correct content, but T5's response is truncated at the final character of the last row ('telemedecine.aphp.org||0.2%||1.' — missing the trailing '0' and closing brace). Qwen generates the full response including the final value '1.0'. T5 hits an output length limit just before completing the last cell, causing a JSON parse failure and scoring it wrong despite being otherwise correct.

T5 correctly produces the table using '||' delimiters with no extra whitespace, matching the label exactly. Qwen produces the same content but uses ' || ' (with surrounding spaces) throughout and adds a trailing newline after the last row, causing the exact-match evaluator to reject it. The structural segmentation is correct in both cases; Qwen's failure is purely a delimiter formatting issue.

Both models correctly identify the three-column structure (letter grade, first numeric value, second numeric value) for this simple six-row table. The consistent pattern makes the task trivial. Qwen uses ' || ' spacing which the evaluator accepts here; T5 uses '||'. No notable differences in approach.

Both models produce correct column segmentation (ID, URL, user, datetime) but both responses are truncated mid-table, failing to complete the full 18-row output. Qwen's response cuts off around row 10 and T5 around row 9. The long URLs in this dataset consume significant output tokens, causing both models to hit generation length limits before finishing. T5 additionally incorrectly splits the datetime column into separate date and time columns (e.g. '13-10-08' and '17:19:27' as two cells instead of one), adding a structural error on top of the truncation.

T5 correctly treats 'Race 1', 'Race 2', etc. as compound tokens (the race number is part of the race label, not a separate column), producing the correct five-column structure. Qwen incorrectly splits 'Race' and the number into two separate columns (e.g. 'Race || 1 || 12:45 PM'), creating a six-column structure that does not match the label. This is a clear semantic segmentation failure: Qwen treats the number as a distinct column value rather than part of the race identifier.

Both models correctly parse this five-column rental cost burden table. T5 adds a trailing space after each percentage value (e.g. '17.40 % ' vs '17.40 %') but the evaluator appears to accept this with whitespace normalization. Qwen's output is a clean exact match. Both get the column structure right.

This is a calendar table where the second row starts with an empty first cell (Sunday falls on day 1, so Monday is blank). The label has '||1||2||3||4||5||6' with a leading empty cell. Qwen correctly places the empty cell at the start of the second row. T5 shifts all values left by one position, placing '1' first and appending an empty cell at the end ('1||2||3||4||5||6||'), reversing the empty cell position. This is a structural off-by-one error in handling leading empty cells.

Both models fail to recognize that Norwegian tax record numbers like '213 441' use a space as a thousands separator, treating each digit group as a separate column. For example, '213 441' should be a single cell but both models split it into '213' and '441' as separate columns. They fail identically: both insert delimiters at every space within the numeric fields, fragmenting the three monetary columns into many more columns. This is a locale-specific number format recognition failure shared by both models.

Both models correctly identify the five-column structure (filename, version, file size, date, time) for this software file listing. The consistent format with clear visual boundaries makes segmentation reliable. Qwen uses ' || ' spacing but is scored as correct; T5 uses '||'. No meaningful differences in approach.

Both models fail on the 'unattached / Nike' affiliation field. Qwen merges the last two columns 'qualified' and 'declared' into a single cell 'qualified declared' without a delimiter, collapsing the sixth column entirely. T5 incorrectly splits 'unattached / Nike' into 'unattached' and '/ Nike' as two separate columns, creating a seven-column structure instead of six. They fail in opposite directions: Qwen under-splits at the end while T5 over-splits within the affiliation field on the slash separator.

Both models are truncated and fail to complete the full 28-row cycling results table. Qwen cuts off around row 13 and T5 around row 14, both running out of output capacity partway through. The column structure (place, time, first name, last name, team, bib number, start time) is correctly identified up to the point of truncation. Additionally Qwen uses ' || ' spacing. The primary failure mode for both is output length truncation on a long table.

Both models correctly parse this train schedule table with six columns (stop number, station name with code, arrival, departure, halt, distance). The structure is nearly identical to idx=115 and equally straightforward. Qwen uses ' || ' spacing but is accepted; T5 uses '||'. No notable differences.

This table has two header-only rows ('Ector County' and an empty-first-cell row with column names) followed by data rows with a varying first-column structure. Qwen partially handles the section header but collapses the empty cell row and mangles the '#TAB R#' tab-separated token. T5 fails more severely by not inserting any delimiters in the first two structural rows at all, and similarly mishandles the embedded '#TAB' annotation. Both fail on the complex multi-level header structure and special whitespace characters embedded in cell values.

The label concatenates player name and position code without any separator (e.g. 'Dexter FowlerCF'). T5 correctly preserves this concatenated format. Qwen incorrectly splits the name from the position code, inserting a delimiter between them (e.g. 'Dexter Fowler||CF'), creating 12 columns instead of 11. Additionally Qwen misspells 'Wilin Rosario' (dropping the 'i' from 'Wilin'). T5 wins because it faithfully reproduces the input's concatenated name-position tokens without attempting to normalize them.

Both models are truncated before completing the 17-row German chess tournament table. The long HTML entity names (e.g. 'ö', 'ü') in club names consume extra tokens. T5 cuts off around row 10 and Qwen also fails to complete the JSON (unterminated string). Qwen additionally converts HTML entities to Unicode escape sequences (e.g. 'ö' becomes '\u00f6') rather than preserving them as literal HTML entities. Both models fail primarily due to output truncation, with Qwen adding an encoding mismatch as a secondary error.

The label has 'Atlanta New Century School' as the full school name in the first column. T5 correctly preserves this as a single token. Qwen incorrectly splits 'Atlanta' as the first cell and 'New Century School' as the second cell, inserting an extra column break after the city name. This creates a four-column structure instead of three. T5 succeeds because it treats the entire phrase as one indivisible school name, while Qwen incorrectly identifies 'Atlanta' as a geographic prefix deserving its own column.

Both models correctly identify the three-column structure (letter grade, first numeric value, second numeric value) for this simple six-row table, consistent with other similar tables in this chunk (idx=109, 118). The pattern is trivially recognizable. Qwen uses ' || ' spacing which is accepted; T5 uses '||'. No notable differences.
